p97.original: Insurance is a method that households and firms use to prevent any single event from having a significant detrimental financial effect. Generally, households or firms with insurance make regular payments, called premiums. The insurance company prices these premiums based on the probability of certain events occurring among a pool of people. Members of the group who then suffer a specified bad experience receive payments from this pool of money.
p97.zh: 保险是家庭和公司用来防止任何单一事件对财务造成重大不利影响的一种方法。一般来说,有保险的家庭或公司定期付款,称为保险费。保险公司根据在人群中发生某些事件的概率对这些保险费进行定价。 然后遭受到某种特别恶劣经历的小组成员从这笔资金中领取款项。

p98.original: Many people have several kinds of insurance: health insurance that pays when they receive medical care; car insurance that pays if their car is in an automobile accident; house or renter’s insurance that pays for stolen possessions or items damaged by fire; and life insurance, which pays for the family if the insured individual dies.  lists a set of insurance markets.
p98.zh: 许多人有几种保险:医疗保险,在接受医疗照顾时支付费用;汽车保险,在汽车事故中支付费用;房屋或租户保险,在被抢走的财产或被火灾损坏的物品上支付费用;人寿保险,在被保险人死亡时支付家属费用。 保险市场包括一系列保险市场。

p111.original: Car is damaged, stolen, or causes damage to others
p111.zh: 汽车受损、被盗或对他人造成损害

p117.original: An injury occurs for which you are partly responsible
p117.zh: 伤害发生时,你应负部分责任

p119.zh: 医生、律师和其他专业人员

p120.original: A poor quality of service is provided that causes harm to others
p120.zh: 服务质量差,对他人造成伤害

p121.original: All insurance involves imperfect information in both an obvious way and in a deeper way. At an obvious level, we cannot predict future events with certainty. For example, we cannot know with certainty who will have a car accident, become ill, die, or have his home robbed in the next year. Imperfect information also applies to estimating the risk that something will happen to any individual. It is difficult for an insurance company to estimate the risk that, say, a particular 20-year-old male driver from New York City will have an accident, because even within that group, some drivers will drive more safely than others. Thus, adverse events occur out of a combination of people’s characteristics and choices that make the risks higher or lower and then the good or bad luck of what actually happens.
p121.zh: 所有保险都以明显的方式和更深入的方式涉及不完善的信息。 显然,我们不能有把握地预测今后发生的事件。 例如,我们无法肯定谁将发生车祸、生病、死亡或明年的家被抢劫。不完整的信息也适用于估计任何个人将发生某种情况的风险。保险公司很难估计,比如说,来自纽约市的20岁男性司机会发生事故,因为即使在这组人中,有些司机的驾驶会比其他司机安全得多。 因此,不良事件是由人们的特征和选择相结合而发生的,这些选择使风险高低,然后是实际发生的好运气或坏运气。

p123.original: A simplified example of automobile insurance might work this way. Suppose we divide a group of 100 drivers into three groups. In a given year, 60 of those people have only a few door dings or chipped paint, which costs $100 each. Another 30 of the drivers have medium-sized accidents that cost an average of $1,000 in damages, and 10 of the drivers have large accidents that cost $15,000 in damages. For the moment, let’s imagine that at the beginning of any year, there is no way of identifying the drivers who are low-risk, medium-risk, or high-risk. The total damage incurred by car accidents in this group of 100 drivers will be $186,000, that is:
p123.zh: 一个简化的汽车保险例子可能这样运作。假设我们把100名司机分成三组 在一年中,其中60人只有几把门 ⁇ 或碎漆,每人花费100美元。另有30名司机发生中等规模的事故,平均损失1000美元,10名司机发生大事故,损失15000美元. 目前,让我们想象一下,在任何一年的年初,都无法识别低风险、中风险或高风险的驾驶员。 这组100名驾驶员因车祸造成的损失共计186 000美元,即:

p124.original: If each of the 100 drivers pays a $1,860 premium each year, the insurance company will collect the $186,000 that is needed to cover the costs of the accidents that occur.
p124.zh: 如果100名司机每人每年支付1,860美元的保险费,保险公司将收取186,000美元,以支付发生的事故的费用。

p125.original: Since insurance companies have such a large number of clients, they are able to negotiate with health care and other service providers for lower rates than the individual would be able to get, thus increasing the benefit to consumers of becoming insured and saving the insurance company itself money when it pays out claims.
p125.zh: 由于保险公司拥有如此众多的客户,它们能够与保健和其他服务提供者谈判,其费率低于个人所能得到的费率,从而增加消费者投保的利益,并在保险公司支付索赔时节省资金。

p126.original: Insurance companies receive income, as  shows, from insurance premiums and investment income. The companies derive income from investing the funds that insurance companies received in the past but did not pay out as insurance claims in prior years. The insurance company receives a rate of return from investing these funds or reserves. The companies typically invest in fairly safe, liquid (easy to convert into cash) investments, as the insurance companies need to be able to readily access these funds when a major disaster strikes.
p126.zh: 如所示,保险公司从保险费和投资收入中获得收入。公司的收入来自投资保险公司过去收到的资金,但在前几年没有作为保险索赔付款。保险公司从这些基金或储备金的投资中获得收益率。公司通常投资相当安全、流动(容易转换成现金)的投资,因为保险公司需要能够在重大灾害发生时随时获得这些资金。

p127.original: An Insurance Company: What Comes In, What Goes Out
p127.zh: 保险公司:什么是进来的,什么是出去的

p129.original: Federal and state governments run a number of insurance programs. Some of the programs look much like private insurance, in the sense that the members of a group make steady payments into a fund, and those in the group who suffer an adverse experience receive payments. Other programs protect against risk, but without an explicit fund set up. Following are some examples.
p129.zh: 联邦和州政府实施了若干保险方案。 一些方案看起来很像私人保险,即一个团体的成员向基金稳定付款,而那些经历不利经历的团体成员则得到付款。 其他方案防止风险,但没有设立明确的基金。 以下是一些例子。

p130.original: Unemployment insurance: Employers in every state pay a small amount for unemployment insurance, which goes into a fund to pay benefits to workers who lose their jobs and do not find new jobs, for a period of time, usually up to six months.
p130.zh: 失业保险:每个州的雇主都为失业保险支付少量费用,这笔费用进入一个基金,用于向失去工作且没有找到新工作的工人支付福利,期限一般为6个月。

p131.original: Pension insurance: Employers that offer pensions to their retired employees are required by law to pay a small fraction of what they are setting aside for pensions to the Pension Benefit Guarantee Corporation, which pays at least some pension benefits to workers if a company goes bankrupt and cannot pay the pensions it has promised.
p131.zh: 养恤金保险:根据法律,向退休雇员提供养恤金的雇主必须向养恤金保障公司支付他们预留的养恤金的一小部分,如果公司破产,无法支付它承诺的养恤金,该公司至少向工人支付一些养恤金。

p132.original: Deposit insurance: Banks are required by law to pay a small fraction of their deposits to the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation, which goes into a fund that pays depositors the value of their bank deposits up to $250,000 (the amount was raised from $100,000 to $250,000 in 2008) if the bank should go bankrupt.
p132.zh: 存款保险:法律规定银行必须向联邦存款保险公司支付一小部分存款,该公司将进入一个基金,向存款人支付其银行存款价值最高达250 000美元(2008年从100 000美元增加到250 000美元),如果银行破产。

p133.original: Workman’s compensation insurance: Employers are required by law to pay a small percentage of the salaries that they pay into funds, typically run at the state level, that pay benefits to workers who suffer an injury on the job.
p133.zh: 工人补偿保险:法律要求雇主支付工资的一小部分,作为支付工伤工人福利的基金,通常在州一级运作。

p134.original: Retirement insurance: All workers pay a percentage of their income into Social Security and into Medicare, which then provides income and health care benefits to the elderly. Social Security and Medicare are not literally “insurance” in the sense that those currently contributing to the fund are not eligible for benefits. They function like insurance, however, in the sense that individuals make regular payments into the programs today in exchange for benefits they will receive in the case of a later event—either becoming old or becoming sick when old. A name for such programs is “social insurance.”
p134.zh: 退休保险:所有工人将其收入的一定比例支付给社会保障和医疗保险,后者随后向老年人提供收入和保健福利。社会保障和医疗保险实际上不是 " 保险 " ,因为目前向基金缴款的人没有资格领取福利。 然而,它们的职能与保险一样,即个人在今天定期向方案付款,以换取以后发生的情况 -- -- 要么老了,要么老了就生病 -- -- 将获得的福利。 这类方案的名称是“社会保险”。

p135.original: The major additional costs to insurance companies, other than the payment of claims, are the costs of running a business: the administrative costs of hiring workers, administering accounts, and processing insurance claims. For most insurance companies, the insurance premiums coming in and the claims payments going out are much larger than the amounts earned by investing money or the administrative costs.
p135.zh: 保险公司除支付索赔外,其他主要额外费用是经营企业的费用:雇用工人、管理账户和处理保险索赔的行政费用。 对大多数保险公司来说,进入的保险费和索赔付款远远大于投资资金或行政费用所得的数额。

p136.original: Thus, while factors like investment income earned on reserves, administrative costs, and groups with different risks complicate the overall picture, a fundamental law of insurance must hold true: The average person’s payments into insurance over time must cover 1) the average person’s claims, 2) the costs of running the company, and 3) leave room for the firm’s profits.
p136.zh: 因此,尽管诸如从储备金、行政费用和不同风险群体获得的投资收入等因素使总体情况复杂化,但保险的基本法必须正确:在一段时间内,普通人向保险支付的款项必须包括1个普通人的索赔,2个公司管理费用,3个公司利润留有余地。

p138.original: Not all of those who purchase insurance face the same risks. Some people may be more likely, because of genetics or personal habits, to fall sick with certain diseases. Some people may live in an area where car theft or home robbery is more likely than in other areas. Some drivers are safer than others. A risk group can be defined as a group that shares roughly the same risks of an adverse event occurring.
p138.zh: 并非所有购买保险的人面临同样的风险。一些人由于遗传学或个人习惯,更可能患上某些疾病。一些人可能生活在一个比其他地区更可能发生偷车或家事抢劫的地区. 有些司机比其他司机安全.风险群体可以定义为大致分担发生不利事件风险的群体。

p139.original: Insurance companies often classify people into risk groups, and charge lower premiums to those with lower risks. If people are not separated into risk groups, then those with low risk must pay for those with high risks. In the simple example of how car insurance works, 60 drivers had very low damage of $100 each, 30 drivers had medium-sized accidents that cost $1,000 each, and 10 of the drivers had large accidents that cost $15,000. If all 100 of these drivers pay the same $1,860, then those with low damages are in effect paying for those with high damages.
p139.zh: 保险公司往往将人归类为风险群体,向风险较低的人收取较低的保险费。 如果不将人们分为风险群体,那么风险低的人就必须为风险高的人付出代价。 在汽车保险如何运作的简单例子中,60名驾驶员的损坏非常低,每人100美元,30名驾驶员的中度事故,每人花费1000美元,10名驾驶员的事故大,花费15000美元. 如果所有100名司机都支付同样的1 860美元,那么,那些损害程度低的司机实际上是为损害程度高的司机支付。

p140.original: If it is possible to classify drivers according to risk group, then the insurance company can charge each group according to its expected losses. For example, the insurance company might charge the 60 drivers who seem safest of all $100 apiece, which is the average value of the damages they cause. Then the intermediate group could pay $1,000 apiece and the high-cost group $15,000 each. When the level of insurance premiums that someone pays is equal to the amount that an average person in that risk group would collect in insurance payments, the level of insurance is said to be “actuarially fair.”
p140.zh: 如果可以按照风险类别对驱动器进行分类,保险公司就可以按照预期损失对每组进行收费. 例如,保险公司可能向60名司机收取费用,他们似乎最安全,每人100美元,这是他们所造成的损害的平均价值。 然后中间组每人可以支付1000美元,而高成本组每人可以支付15000美元. 如果某人支付的保险费水平相当于该风险群体中普通人将收取的保险金,保险水平就被认为“实际上公平”。

p141.original: Classifying people into risk groups can be controversial. For example, if someone had a major automobile accident last year, should the insurance company classify that person as a high-risk driver who is likely to have similar accidents in the future, or as a low-risk driver who was just extremely unlucky? The driver is likely to claim to be low-risk, and thus someone who should be in a risk group with those who pay low insurance premiums in the future. The insurance company is likely to believe that, on average, having a major accident is a signal of being a high-risk driver, and thus try to charge this driver higher insurance premiums. The next two sections discuss the two major problems of imperfect information in insurance markets—called moral hazard and adverse selection. Both problems arise from attempts to categorize those purchasing insurance into risk groups.
p141.zh: 将人们归类为风险群体可能会引起争议. 例如,如果某人去年发生重大汽车事故,保险公司是否应该将此人归类为今后可能发生类似事故的高风险驾驶员,还是将此人归类为极不幸运的低风险驾驶员?驾驶员可能声称风险低,因此应该与未来支付低保费的人一起处于风险组中.保险公司可能认为,平均而言,发生重大事故是高风险驾驶员的信号,因此试图向该驾驶员收取更高的保险费.下两节讨论保险市场信息不完善的两个主要问题,即所谓的道德风险和不利的选择。 这两个问题都产生于试图将购买保险的人归类为风险群体。

p143.original: Moral hazard refers to the case when people engage in riskier behavior with insurance than they would if they did not have insurance. For example, if you have health insurance that covers the cost of visiting the doctor, you may be less likely to take precautions against catching an illness that might require a doctor’s visit. If you have car insurance, you will worry less about driving or parking your car in ways that make it more likely to get dented. In another example, a business without insurance might install absolute top-level security and fire sprinkler systems to guard against theft and fire. If it is insured, that same business might only install a minimum level of security and fire sprinkler systems.
p143.zh: 道德危险是指人们在保险方面采取比没有保险时风险更大的行为的情况。 例如,如果您有医疗保险支付医生的就诊费用,您可能不太可能采取预防措施,避免感染可能需要医生就诊的疾病。 如果你有汽车保险, 你会少担心开车或停车的方式 使它更容易被凹陷。 在另一个例子中,没有保险的企业可能安装绝对的顶层安全和消防喷洒系统,以防止盗窃和火灾。 如果投保,同一企业可能只安装最低限度的安全和消防喷洒系统。

p144.original: We cannot eliminate moral hazard, but insurance companies have some ways of reducing its effect. Investigations to prevent insurance fraud are one way of reducing the extreme cases of moral hazard. Insurance companies can also monitor certain kinds of behavior. To return to the example from above, they might offer a business a lower rate on property insurance if the business installs a top-level security and fire sprinkler system and has those systems inspected once a year.
p144.zh: 我们不能消除道德风险,但保险公司可以采取一些办法减少其影响。为防止保险欺诈而进行的调查是减少极端道德风险案件的一种方式。保险公司也可以监测某些种类的行为. 从上面再举一个例子,如果企业安装了顶级的安全和消防喷洒系统,并且每年检查一次这些系统,它们可能会为企业提供较低的财产保险费率。

p145.original: Another method to reduce moral hazard is to require the injured party to pay a share of the costs. For example, insurance policies often have deductibles, which is an amount that the insurance policyholder must pay out of their own pocket before the insurance coverage starts paying. For example, auto insurance might pay for all losses greater than $500. Health insurance policies often have a copayment, in which the policyholder must pay a small amount. For example, a person might have to pay $20 for each doctor visit, and the insurance company would cover the rest. Another method of cost sharing is coinsurance, which means that the insurance company covers a certain percentage of the cost. For example, insurance might pay for 80% of the costs of repairing a home after a fire, but the homeowner would pay the other 20%.
p145.zh: 减少道德风险的另一种方法是要求受害方支付一定比例的费用. 例如,保险单往往有扣减额,这是保险投保人必须在保险开始支付之前从自己的口袋中支付的数额。 例如,汽车保险可能支付超过500美元的所有损失。健康保险单往往有共同支付,投保人必须支付少量费用。 例如,一个人可能每次看医生都要付20美元,其余费用由保险公司承担。另一种分担费用的方法是共同保险,这意味着保险公司承担一定比例的费用. 例如,保险可能支付房屋火灾后修复费用的80%,但房屋所有人将支付另外20%的费用。

p146.original: All of these forms of cost sharing discourage moral hazard, because people know that they will have to pay something out of their own pocket when they make an insurance claim. The effect can be powerful. One prominent study found that when people face moderate deductibles and copayments for their health insurance, they consume about one-third less in medical care than people who have complete insurance and do not pay anything out of pocket, presumably because deductibles and copayments reduce the level of moral hazard. However, those who consumed less health care did not seem to have any difference in health status.
p146.zh: 所有这些费用分摊形式都阻止了道德风险,因为人们知道,在提出保险要求时,他们必须自掏腰包支付费用。效果可以很强.一项突出的研究发现,当人们面临适量扣除和共同支付健康保险时,他们在医疗方面的消费比那些有完全保险和没有从口袋中支付任何费用的人少约三分之一,这大概是因为扣除和共同支付降低了道德风险的程度。 然而,那些消费较少的保健者似乎在健康状况上没有任何差别。

p147.original: A final way of reducing moral hazard, which is especially applicable to health care, is to focus on healthcare incentives of providers  rather than consumers. Traditionally, most health care in the United States has been provided on a fee-for-service basis, which means that medical care providers are paid for the services they provide and are paid more if they provide additional services. However, in the last decade or so, the structure of healthcare provision has shifted to an emphasis on health maintenance organizations (HMOs). A health maintenance organization (HMO) provides healthcare that receives a fixed amount per person enrolled in the plan—regardless of how many services are provided. In this case, a patient with insurance has an incentive to demand more care, but the healthcare provider, which is receiving only a fixed payment, has an incentive to reduce the moral hazard problem by limiting the quantity of care provided—as long as it will not lead to worse health problems and higher costs later. Today, many doctors are paid with some combination of managed care and fee-for-service; that is, a flat amount per patient, but with additional payments for the treatment of certain health conditions.
p147.zh: 减少道德风险的最后办法尤其适用于保健,是注重对服务提供者而不是消费者的保健奖励。传统上,美国大多数保健都是按收费服务方式提供的,这意味着医疗服务提供者为其提供的服务付费,如果提供额外服务,则得到更多的报酬。 然而,在过去十年左右的时间里,保健提供结构已转向强调保健维持组织。健康维持组织提供保健,无论提供多少服务,每名登记在计划内的人可得到固定数额的保健服务。 在这种情况下,有保险的病人有需要更多护理的动机,但只获得固定付款的保健提供者有通过限制所提供护理的数量减少道德危害问题的动机——只要这不会导致更糟糕的健康问题和以后的更高成本。 如今,许多医生的薪酬都由管理下的护理和收费服务相结合,也就是说,每个病人都有一笔固定的金额,但对某些健康状况的治疗需要额外付款。

p148.original: Imperfect information is the cause of the moral hazard problem. If an insurance company had perfect information on risk, it could simply raise its premiums every time an insured party engages in riskier behavior. However, an insurance company cannot monitor all the risks that people take all the time and so, even with various checks and cost sharing, moral hazard will remain a problem.
p148.zh: 信息不完善是道德危害问题的原因。 如果保险公司掌握关于风险的完美信息,那么它就能够简单地在投保方从事风险更大行为时每次提高保险费。 然而,保险公司无法监测人们所承受的所有风险,因此,即使通过各种检查和费用分担,道德风险仍将是一个问题。

p149.original: Visit this website to read about the relationship between health care and behavioral economics.
p149.zh: 访问此网站阅读保健与行为经济学的关系.

p151.original: Adverse selection refers to the problem in which insurance buyers  have more information about whether they are high-risk or low-risk than the insurance company does. This creates an asymmetric information problem for the insurance company because buyers who are high-risk tend to want to buy more insurance, without letting the insurance company know about their higher risk. For example, someone purchasing health insurance or life insurance probably knows more about their family’s health history than an insurer can reasonably find out even with a costly investigation. Someone purchasing car insurance may know that they are a high-risk driver who has not yet had a major accident—but it is hard for the insurance company to collect information about how people actually drive.
p151.zh: 逆向选择是指保险买家比保险公司更了解他们是否高风险或低风险的问题. 这给保险公司造成了一个不对称的信息问题,因为高风险的买家往往想购买更多的保险,而不让保险公司知道他们的风险较高. 例如,购买健康保险或人寿保险的人可能比保险人更了解他们的家庭健康史,即使经过昂贵的调查,也更能合理发现。购买汽车保险的人可能知道他们是一个高风险司机,还没有发生重大事故,但保险公司很难收集到有关人们实际驾驶方式的信息。

p152.original: To understand how adverse selection can strangle an insurance market, recall the situation of 100 drivers who are buying automobile insurance, where 60 drivers had very low damages of $100 each, 30 drivers had medium-sized accidents that cost $1,000 each, and 10 of the drivers had large accidents that cost $15,000. That would equal $186,000 in total payouts by the insurance company. Imagine that, while the insurance company knows the overall size of the losses, it cannot identify the high-risk, medium-risk, and low-risk drivers. However, the drivers themselves know their risk groups. Since there is asymmetric information between the insurance company and the drivers, the insurance company would likely set the price of insurance at $1,860 per year, to cover the average loss (not including the cost of overhead and profit). The result is that those with low risks of only $100 will likely decide not to buy insurance; after all, it makes no sense for them to pay $1,860 per year when they are likely only to experience losses of $100. Those with medium risks of a $1,000 accident will not buy insurance either. Therefore, the insurance company ends up only selling insurance for $1,860 to high-risk drivers who will average $15,000 in claims apiece, and as a consequence, the insurance company ends up losing considerable money. If the insurance company tries to raise its premiums to cover the losses of those with high risks, then those with low or medium risks will be even more discouraged from buying insurance.
p152.zh: 为了了解不利的选择如何可以扼杀保险市场,回顾一下100名正在购买汽车保险的司机的情况,60名司机每辆损失非常低100美元,30名司机每辆花费1000美元的中型事故,10名司机每辆花费15 000美元的大型事故. 这相当于保险公司总付款额的186,000美元。想象一下,虽然保险公司知道损失的总体规模,但它无法识别高风险,中风险,低风险的驱动力. 然而,司机本身也了解他们的风险群体。 由于保险公司和驾驶员之间的信息不对称,保险公司很可能将保险价格定为每年1,860美元,以弥补平均损失(不包括间接费用和利润)。结果是,风险低但只有100美元的人可能决定不购买保险;毕竟,他们每年支付1 860美元是毫无意义的,因为他们可能只遭受100美元的损失。发生1000美元事故的中度风险者也不会购买保险。 因此,保险公司最后只向高风险司机出售1 860美元的保险,这些司机每人索赔平均为15 000美元,因此,保险公司最终损失了大笔资金。 如果保险公司试图提高保险费以弥补高风险者的损失,那么低风险或中风险者将更不愿意购买保险。

p153.original: Rather than face such a situation of adverse selection, the insurance company may decide not to sell insurance in this market at all. If potential buyers are to receive insurance, then one of two things must happen. First, the insurance company might find some way of separating insurance buyers into risk groups with some degree of accuracy and charging them accordingly, which in practice often means that the insurance company tries not to sell insurance to those who may pose high risks. Another scenario is that those with low risks must buy insurance, even if they have to pay more than the actuarially fair amount for their risk group. The notion that people can be required to purchase insurance raises the issue of government laws and regulations that influence the insurance industry.
p153.zh: 保险公司不应面临这种不利的选择情况,而可决定根本不在这一市场出售保险。 如果潜在买家要接受保险,那么必须发生两件事之一。 首先,保险公司可能会找到某种方法,将保险购买者以某种程度的准确性划分成风险组,并据此收取费用,这在实践中往往意味着保险公司试图不向那些可能构成高风险的人出售保险.另一种情况是,低风险者必须购买保险,即使他们必须为其风险群体支付比精算公允数额更多的保险。人可以被要求购买保险的概念提出了影响保险业的政府法律法规问题.

p154.original: U.S. Health Care in an International Context
p154.zh: 美国. 国际背景下的保健

p155.original: The United States is the only high-income country in the world where private firms pay and provide for most health insurance. Greater government involvement in the provision of health insurance is one possible way of addressing moral hazard and adverse selection problems.
p155.zh: 美国是世界上唯一一个私人公司支付和提供大多数健康保险的高收入国家。 政府更多地参与提供健康保险是解决道德危害和不利选择问题的可能办法之一。

p156.original: The moral hazard problem with health insurance is that when people have insurance, they will demand higher quantities of health care. In the United States, private healthcare insurance tends to encourage an ever-greater demand for healthcare services, which healthcare providers are happy to fulfill.  shows that on a per-person basis, U.S. healthcare spending towers above healthcare spending of other countries. Note that while healthcare expenditures in the United States are far higher than healthcare expenditures in other countries, the health outcomes in the United States, as measured by life expectancy and lower rates of childhood mortality, tend to be lower. Health outcomes, however, may not be significantly affected by healthcare expenditures. Many studies have shown that a country’s health is more closely related to diet, exercise, and genetic factors than to healthcare expenditure. This fact further emphasizes that the United States is spending very large amounts on medical care with little obvious health gain.
p156.zh: 健康保险的道德危害问题是,人们有保险时,会要求更多的保健。在美国,私人健康保险往往鼓励对保健服务的需求越来越大,而保健提供者也乐于满足这种需求。 这表明,美国保健支出塔在人均基础上高于其他国家的保健支出。请注意,虽然美国的保健支出远高于其他国家的保健支出,但以预期寿命和较低儿童死亡率衡量的美国保健成果往往较低。 但是,保健开支可能不会对健康结果产生重大影响。 许多研究表明,一国的健康与饮食、锻炼和遗传因素的关系比与保健支出的关系更为密切。这一事实进一步强调,美国在医疗方面花费了大量资金,而医疗收益却很少。

p157.original: In the U.S. health insurance market, the main way of solving this adverse selection problem is that health insurance is often sold through groups based on place of employment, or, under The Affordable Care Act, from a state government sponsored health exchange market. From an insurance company’s point of view, selling insurance through an employer mixes together a group of people—some with high risks of future health problems and some with lower risks—and thus reduces the insurance firm’s fear of attracting only those who have high risks. However, many small companies do not provide health insurance to their employees, and many lower-paying jobs do not include health insurance. Even after we take into account all U.S. government programs that provide health insurance for the elderly and people experiencing poverty, approximately 31 million Americans were without health insurance in 2020. While a government-controlled system can avoid the adverse selection problem entirely by providing at least basic health insurance for all, another option is to mandate that all Americans buy health insurance from some provider by preventing providers from denying individuals based on preexisting conditions. The Patient Protection and Affordable Care Act adopted this approach, which we will discuss later on in this chapter.
p157.zh: 在美国健康保险市场中,解决这一不利选择问题的主要途径是健康保险常常通过基于就业地点的团体出售,或者根据"负担得起的护理法",从州政府赞助的保健交流市场出售. 从保险公司的角度来看,通过雇主出售保险将一群人混为一谈——有些人未来健康问题的风险很高,有些人风险较低——从而减少了保险公司只吸引那些高风险者的恐惧。 然而,许多小公司不为其雇员提供医疗保险,许多低薪工作不包括医疗保险.即使在我们考虑到美国政府为老年人和穷人提供医疗保险的所有方案后,2020年约有3100万美国人没有医疗保险. 虽然政府控制的系统可以完全通过为所有人提供至少基本医疗保险来避免不利的选择问题,但另一种选择是强制要求所有美国人从某些提供商购买健康保险,防止提供商根据先前存在的条件拒绝个人参保. 《患者保护和负担得起的护理法》采用了这一办法,我们将在本章稍后讨论。

p158.original: A Comparison of Health Care Spending per Person, Life Expectancy at Birth, and Infant Mortality, 2020
p158.zh: 2020年人均医疗保健支出、出生时预期寿命和婴儿死亡率比较

p189.original: At its best, the largely private U.S. system of health insurance and healthcare delivery provides an extraordinarily high quality of care, along with generating a seemingly endless parade of life-saving innovations. However, the system also struggles to control its high costs and to provide basic medical care to all. Compared to the United States, other countries have lower costs, more equal access, and better mortality outcomes, but they often struggle to provide rapid access to health care and to offer the near-miracles of the most up-to-date medical care. The challenge is a healthcare system that strikes the right balance between quality, access, and cost.
p189.zh: 美国的健康保险和医疗保健提供制度基本上是私人的,它提供质量极高的护理,同时产生似乎无休止的拯救生命的创新。 然而,该系统也难以控制其高昂的费用,也难以向所有人提供基本医疗护理。与美国相比,其他国家成本较低,获得机会更加平等,死亡率结果更好,但它们往往难以迅速提供医疗保健,并提供最新医疗护理的近乎奇迹。挑战在于医疗保健系统在质量、获取机会和成本之间保持适当的平衡。

p191.original: The U.S. insurance industry is primarily regulated at the state level. Since 1871 there has been a National Association of Insurance Commissioners that brings together these state regulators to exchange information and strategies. The state insurance regulators typically attempt to accomplish two things: to keep the price of insurance low and to ensure that everyone has insurance. These goals, however, can conflict with each other and also become easily entangled in politics.
p191.zh: 美国的保险业主要是在州一级进行监管. 自1871年以来,有一个全国保险专员协会,召集这些州监管机构交流信息和战略。国家保险监管机构通常试图完成两件事:保持保险价格低廉和确保每个人都有保险。 然而,这些目标可能相互冲突,也容易陷入政治的纠缠之中。

p192.original: If insurance premiums are set at actuarially fair levels, so that people end up paying an amount that accurately reflects their risk group, certain people will end up paying considerable amounts. For example, if health insurance companies were trying to cover people who already have a chronic disease like AIDS, or who were elderly, they would charge these groups very high premiums for health insurance, because their expected health care costs are quite high. Women in the age bracket 18–44 consume, on average, about 65% more in health care spending than men. Young male drivers have more car accidents than young female drivers. Thus, actuarially fair insurance would tend to charge young men much more for car insurance than young women. Because people in high-risk groups would find themselves charged so heavily for insurance, they might choose not to buy insurance at all.
p192.zh: 如果将保险费确定在精算公平的水平上,以便人们最终支付准确反映其风险群体的数额,那么某些人最终将支付相当数额的保险费。 例如,如果健康保险公司试图为已经患有艾滋病等慢性病的人或老年人提供保险,它们就会向这些群体收取很高的健康保险费,因为他们的预期保健费用相当高。18至44岁年龄段的妇女平均在保健支出方面的消耗比男子多约65%。年轻男性驾驶员的车祸比年轻女性驾驶员多. 因此,精算公平的保险往往比青年妇女要多得多地收取青年男子的汽车保险费用。 由于高风险群体中的人会发现自己被收取如此沉重的保险费,他们可能选择根本不购买保险.

p193.original: State insurance regulators have sometimes reacted by passing rules that attempt to set low premiums for insurance. Over time, however, the fundamental law of insurance must hold: the average amount individuals receive cannot exceed the average amount paid in premiums. When rules are passed to keep premiums low, insurance companies try to avoid insuring any high-risk or even medium-risk parties. If a state legislature passes strict rules requiring insurance companies to sell to everyone at low prices, the insurance companies always have the option of withdrawing from doing business in that state. For example, the insurance regulators in New Jersey are well-known for attempting to keep auto insurance premiums low, and more than 20 different insurance companies stopped doing business in the state in the late 1990s and early 2000s. Similarly, in 2009, State Farm announced that it was withdrawing from selling property insurance in Florida.
p193.zh: 国家保险管理机构有时通过规则作出反应,这些规则试图规定较低的保险费。 但是,随着时间的推移,保险基本法必须维持:个人得到的平均金额不能超过以保险费支付的平均金额。 当通过规则以保持低保费时,保险公司试图避免为任何高风险甚至中风险方提供保险。 如果一个州立法机构通过严格的规则,要求保险公司以低价向所有人出售,保险公司总是可以选择退出该州的业务. 例如,新泽西州的保险监管机构以试图降低汽车保险费而闻名,20多个不同的保险公司在1990年代末和2000年代初停止了在该州的营业. 同样,2009年,州立农场宣布退出佛罗里达州出售财产保险.

p194.original: In short, government regulators cannot force companies to charge low prices and provide high levels of insurance coverage—and thus take losses—for a sustained period of time. If insurance premiums are set below the actuarially fair level for a certain group, some other group will have to make up the difference. There are two other groups who can make up the difference: taxpayers or other insurance buyers.
p194.zh: 简言之,政府监管者不能强迫公司收取低价,提供高水平的保险,从而承受长期的损失。 如果将某一群体的保险费定在精算公平水平以下,则某些其他群体必须补足差额。另有两种群体可以弥补差额:纳税人或其他保险买家.

p195.original: In some industries, the U.S. government has decided free markets will not provide insurance at an affordable price, and so the government pays for it directly. For example, private health insurance is too expensive for many people whose incomes are too low. To combat this, the U.S. government, together with the states, runs the Medicaid program, which provides health care to those with low incomes. Private health insurance also does not work well for the elderly, because their average health care costs can be very high. Thus, the U.S. government started the Medicare program, which provides health insurance to all those over age 65. Other government-funded health-care programs are aimed at military veterans, as an added benefit, and children in families with relatively low incomes.
p195.zh: 在一些行业中,美国政府决定自由市场不会以负担得起的价格提供保险,因此政府直接支付. 例如,对于收入太低的许多人来说,私人健康保险费用太高。 为了打击这种情况,美国政府与各州共同实施医疗补助方案,向低收入者提供医疗保健。私人健康保险对老年人也不太有效,因为他们的平均保健费用可能很高。 因此,美国政府启动了医疗保险计划,为所有65岁以上的人提供医疗保险. 其他由政府资助的保健方案针对的是退伍军人和收入相对较低的家庭中的儿童,作为额外福利。

p196.original: Another common government intervention in insurance markets is to require that everyone buy certain kinds of insurance. For example, most states legally require car owners to buy auto insurance. Likewise, when a bank loans someone money to buy a home, the person is typically required to have homeowner’s insurance, which protects against fire and other physical damage (like hailstorms) to the home. A legal requirement that everyone must buy insurance means that insurance companies do not need to worry that those with low risks will avoid buying insurance. Since insurance companies do not need to fear adverse selection, they can set their prices based on an average for the market, and those with lower risks will, to some extent, end up subsidizing those with higher risks. However, even when laws are passed requiring people to purchase insurance, insurance companies cannot be compelled to sell insurance to everyone who asks—at least not at low cost. Thus, insurance companies will still try to avoid selling insurance to those with high risks whenever possible.
p196.zh: 政府在保险市场上的另一项共同干预是要求每个人购买某些类型的保险. 例如,大多数州在法律上要求汽车所有人购买汽车保险. 同样,当银行向某人贷款购买住房时,通常要求此人拥有房主的保险,防止火灾和其他物质损害(如冰雹)。人人必须购买保险的法律要求意味着保险公司不必担心风险低的人会避免购买保险。 由于保险公司不需要担心不利的选择,它们可以按照市场的平均价格来定价,风险较低的公司将在某种程度上最终补贴风险较高的公司。 然而,即使在通过法律要求购买保险时,保险公司也不能被迫将保险出售给每一个要求——至少不是低价——的人。 因此,保险公司仍将尽量避免向高风险者出售保险。

p197.original: The government cannot pass laws that make the problems of moral hazard and adverse selection disappear, but the government can make political decisions that certain groups should have insurance, even though the private market would not otherwise provide that insurance. Also, the government can impose the costs of that decision on taxpayers or on other buyers of insurance.
p197.zh: 政府不能通过法律,使道德危害和不利选择的问题消失,但政府可以作出政治决定,即某些群体应该有保险,即使私人市场不提供这种保险。 此外,政府可以将这一决定的费用强加给纳税人或其他保险购买者。

p198.original: The Patient Protection and Affordable Care Act
p198.zh: 《病人保护和负担得起的护理法》

p199.original: In March of 2010, President Obama signed into law the Patient Protection and Affordable Care Act  (PPACA). The government started to phase in this highly contentious law over time starting in October of 2013. The goal of the act is to bring the United States closer to universal coverage. Some of the key features of the plan include:
p199.zh: 2010年3月,奥巴马总统签署了《患者保护和负担得起的护理法》,使之成为法律。 从2013年10月开始,政府开始逐步实施这一极具争议性的法律。该法案的目标是使美国更接近普及。 该计划的一些关键特征包括:

p200.original: Individual mandate: All individuals, who do not receive health care through their employer or through a government program (for example, Medicare), were required to have health insurance or pay a fine. The individual mandate's goal was to reduce the adverse selection problem and keep prices down by requiring all consumers—even the healthiest ones—to have health insurance. Without the need to guard against adverse selection (whereby only the riskiest consumers buy insurance) by raising prices, health insurance companies could provide more reasonable plans to their customers. At the beginning of 2019, the fine for not having health insurance was eliminated.
p200.zh: 个人任务:所有不通过雇主或通过政府方案(例如医疗保险)获得医疗保健的人,都必须有医疗保险或缴纳罚款。个别任务的目标是减少不利的选择问题,降低价格,要求所有消费者——即使是最健康的人——都享有健康保险。无需通过提高价格来防止不利的选择(只有风险最大的消费者才能购买保险),健康保险公司可以向其客户提供更合理的计划。2019年初,取消对没有医疗保险的罚款.

p201.original: Each state is required to have health insurance exchanges, or utilize the federal exchange, whereby insurance companies compete for business. The goal of the exchanges is to improve competition in the market for health insurance.
p201.zh: 各州必须建立健康保险交易所,或利用联邦交易所,保险公司通过该交易所进行商业竞争。交易所的目标是改善健康保险市场的竞争。

p202.original: Employer mandate: All employers with more than 50 employees must offer health insurance to their employees.
p202.zh: 雇主授权:雇员超过50名的所有雇主必须为其雇员提供健康保险。

p203.original: The Affordable Care Act (ACA) is funded through additional taxes that include:
p203.zh: 《可负担照料法》的资金来自额外的税收,包括:

p204.original: Increasing the Medicare tax by 0.9 percent and adding a 3.8 percent tax on unearned income for high income taxpayers.
p204.zh: 将医疗保险税提高0.9%,并对高收入纳税人的未收收入增加3.8%的税。

p205.original: Charging an annual fee on health insurance providers.
p205.zh: 向医疗保险提供商收取年费.

p206.original: Imposing other taxes such as a 2.3% tax on manufacturers and importers of certain medical devices.
p206.zh: 对某些医疗器械的制造商和进口商征收其他税种,如2.3%。

p207.original: Many people and politicians, including Donald Trump, have sought to overturn the bill. Those who oppose the bill believe it violates an individual’s right to choose whether to have insurance or not. In 2012, a number of states challenged the law on the basis that the individual mandate provision is unconstitutional. In June 2012, the U.S. Supreme Court ruled in a 5–4 decision that the individual mandate is actually a tax, so it is constitutional as the federal government has the right to tax the populace. At the same time, some of the taxes that were implemented as part of the ACA have been eliminated.
p207.zh: 包括唐纳德·特朗普在内的许多人和政治家都试图推翻该法案. 反对法案的人认为该法案侵犯了个人选择是否投保的权利.2012年,一些州以个别任务规定违宪为由对该法提出质疑.2012年6月,美国.最高法院在5–4裁决中裁定,个人授权实际上是一种税收,因此这是符合宪法的,因为联邦政府有权对民众征税。 同时,部分作为ACA的一部分实施的税收被取消.

p208.original: What’s the Big Deal with Obamacare?
p208.zh: 奥巴马护理有什么大不了的?

p209.original: What is it that the Affordable Care Act (ACA) will actually do? To begin with, we should note that it is a massively complex law, with a large number of parts, some of which the Obama administration implemented immediately, and others that the government is supposed to phase in every year from 2013 through 2020.  Three of these parts are coverage for the uninsured—those without health insurance, coverage for individuals with preexisting conditions, and the so-called employer and individual mandates, which require employers to offer and people to purchase health insurance. Under the Trump administration, several components of the ACA were repealed or overhauled, while under the Biden administration (and with the support of a majority of the population) the ACA has continued as a major element in provision of health care in the United States.
p209.zh: 《可负担照料法》实际上会做什么? 首先,我们应该注意到,这是一个大规模复杂的法律,它有很多部分,其中一些是奥巴马政府立即实施的,还有一些是政府从2013年到2020年每年都要逐步实施的法律。 其中三部分是无保险者——没有健康保险者、有原有条件的个人以及所谓的雇主和个人授权的保险,这些要求雇主提供和人们购买健康保险。 在特朗普政府治下,ACA的几个组成部分被废除或整顿,而在拜登政府治下(并在大多数民众的支持下),ACA继续作为美国提供医疗服务的一个主要内容.

p210.original:
As we noted in the chapter, people face ever-increasing healthcare costs in the United States.
Over the years, the ranks of the uninsured in the United States have grown as rising prices have pushed employers and individuals out of the market.  Insurance companies have increasingly used pre-existing medical conditions to determine if someone is high risk, for whom insurance companies either charge higher prices, or they choose to deny insurance coverage to these individuals.  Whatever the cause, we noted at the beginning of the chapter that prior to the ACA, more than 32 million Americans were uninsured.  People who are uninsured tend to use emergency rooms for treatment—the most expensive form of healthcare, which has contributed significantly to rising costs.
p210.zh: 正如我们在本章中指出的那样,在美国,人们面临着不断增加的保健费用。多年来,美国未投保者的人数不断增长,因为价格上涨将雇主和个人赶出市场。保险公司越来越多地利用先前存在的医疗条件来确定某人是否具有高风险,保险公司要么为谁收取较高的价格,要么选择拒绝为这些人提供保险。 无论原因为何,我们在本章开头指出,在ACA之前,超过3200万美国人没有保险. 没有保险的人往往使用急诊室进行治疗,这是最昂贵的保健形式,这在很大程度上导致了费用的增长。

p211.original: The ACA introduced regulations designed to control increases in healthcare costs.  One example is a cap on the amount healthcare providers can spend on administrative costs. Another is a requirement that healthcare providers switch to electronic medical records (EMRs), which will reduce administrative costs.
p211.zh: ACA引入了旨在控制医疗费用增加的条例。一个例子是,对保健提供者在行政费用方面的支出额规定了上限。另一项要求是,保健提供者必须转用电子病历,这将减少行政费用。

p212.original: The ACA required that states establish health insurance exchanges, or markets, where people without health insurance, and businesses that do not provide it for their employees, can shop for different insurance plans. The purpose of these exchanges was to increase competition in insurance markets and thus reduce prices of policies.
p212.zh: ACA要求各州建立健康保险交易所或市场,没有健康保险的人和不为其雇员提供健康保险的企业可以购买不同的保险计划。 这些交易所的目的是增加保险市场的竞争,从而降低保险单的价格。

p213.original: Finally, the ACA mandated that people with preexisting conditions could no longer be denied health insurance. The U.S. Department of Health and Human Services estimates that the those without insurance in the US  has fallen from 20.3% in 2012 to 11.5% in 2016. Accordingly, 20 million Americans gained coverage under the ACA. According to the Census, as of 2020, the share of the population without health insurance had fallen to 8.6%. So the ACA has resulted in a decline in the percentage of Americans without health insurance by almost 60%.
p213.zh: 最后,ACA规定,已经存在疾病的人不能再被剥夺健康保险。 美国.卫生与公众服务部估计,美国无保险者已从2012年的20.3%下降到2016年的11.5%。 因此,2 000万美国人获得了ACA的保险。 根据人口普查,截至2020年,无医疗保险人口的比例下降到8.6%. 因此ACA导致没有医疗保险的美国人的比例下降了近60%.

p214.original: What was the cost of this increased coverage and how was it paid?  An insurance policy works by insuring against the possibility of needing healthcare.  If there are high risk individuals in the insurance pool, the pool must be expanded to include enough low risk individuals to keep average premiums affordable.  To that end, the ACA imposed the individual mandate, requiring all individuals to purchase insurance (or pay a penalty) whether they were high risk or not.  Many young adults would choose to skip health insurance since the likelihood of their needing significant healthcare is small. The individual mandate brought in a significant amount of money to pay for the ACA. However, despite the elimination of the penalty for not having insurance, ACA coverage has continued to increase. In addition, there were three other funding sources. The ACA took $716 billion which otherwise would have gone to Medicare spending. The ACA also increased the Medicare tax that wealthy Americans paid by an additional 0.9%. Despite these funding sources, the Congressional Budget Office estimates that the ACA will increase the federal debt by $137 billion over the next decade.
p214.zh: 增加保险的费用是什么? 如何支付?一项保险政策通过防止需要医疗保健的可能性而起作用。 如果保险池中存在高风险个人,则必须扩大该池,以包括足够低风险个人,使平均保费能够负担得起。 为此,ACA规定了个人的任务,要求所有个人购买保险(或支付罚款),无论他们是否高风险。 许多年轻人会选择放弃医疗保险,因为他们需要大量医疗保健的可能性很小。个别任务带来大量资金来支付《农产品协议》的费用。 然而,尽管取消了对没有保险的处罚,但ACA的保险范围继续扩大。 此外,还有其他三个供资来源。ACA耗资7,160亿美元,否则就花在了医疗计划的开支上。ACA还增加了美国富人支付的医疗保障税,额外增加了0.9%. 尽管有这些资金来源,国会预算办公室估计,ACA在未来十年内将联邦债务增加1,370亿美元.

p215.original: The impact of the Patient Protection and Affordable Care Act has been a rise in Americans with health insurance. However, due to the increased taxes to pay for the ACA and the increased deficit spending, the ACA faces continued opposition. The Trump administration vowed to repeal it on the campaign trail but no alternative bill has made its way before congress. Only time will tell if the Affordable Care Act will leave a legacy or will quickly be swept by the wayside, jeopardizing the 20 million newly insured Americans.
p215.zh: 《患者保护和负担得起的护理法》的影响在有医疗保险的美国人中有所上升。 然而,由于支付ACA的税收增加和赤字支出增加,ACA继续面临反对.特朗普政府誓言在竞选路线上废除,但国会之前没有任何替代法案成功. 只有时间才能知道 《可负担的护理法》是否会留下遗产 或者会很快被抛到一边 危及到两千万新参保的美国人

p216.original: At the time of this writing, the final impact of the Patient Protection and Affordable Care Act is not clear.  Millions of previously uninsured Americans now have coverage, but the increased taxes to pay for ACA and increased deficit spending have created significant political opposition. Whether or not that opposition eventually succeeds in overturning the ACA remains to be seen.
p216.zh: 在编写本报告时,《患者保护和负担得起的护理法》的最终影响尚不明确。数百万以前没有保险的美国人现在有保险,但为ACA支付税的增加和赤字支出的增加造成了重大的政治反对.反对派最终能否推翻《反腐败协定》仍有待观察。

p218.original: Insurance is a way of sharing risk. People in a group pay premiums for insurance against some unpleasant event, and those in the group who actually experience the unpleasant event then receive some compensation. The fundamental law of insurance is that what the average person pays in over time cannot be less than what the average person gets out. In an actuarially fair insurance policy, the premiums that a person pays to the insurance company are the same as the average amount of benefits for a person in that risk group. Moral hazard arises in insurance markets because those who are insured against a risk will have less reason to take steps to avoid the costs from that risk.
p218.zh: 保险是一种分担风险的方式。团体中的人为一些不愉快事件支付保险费,团体中实际经历不愉快事件的人随后获得一些补偿.基本保险法是,在一段时间内,普通人支付的费用不得少于普通人获得的费用。 在精算公平的保险单中,个人向保险公司支付的保险费与该风险群体中个人的平均福利金额相同。道德风险出现在保险市场,因为那些受风险保险的人没有多少理由采取措施避免风险带来的费用。

p219.original: Many insurance policies have deductibles, copayments, or coinsurance. A deductible is the maximum amount that the policyholder must pay out-of-pocket before the insurance company pays the rest of the bill. A copayment is a flat fee that an insurance policy-holder must pay before receiving services. Coinsurance requires the policyholder to pay a certain percentage of costs. Deductibles, copayments, and coinsurance reduce moral hazard by requiring the insured party to bear some of the costs before collecting insurance benefits.
p219.zh: 许多保险单有扣除额、共同支付额或共同保险额。 可扣除金额是指投保人在保险公司支付其余账单之前必须自付的最高限额。共同付费是指保险投保人在接受服务前必须缴纳的固定费用。共同保险要求投保人支付一定比例的费用. 可扣减、共同支付和共同保险通过要求投保方在领取保险福利之前承担部分费用,从而减少道德风险。

p220.original: In a fee-for-service health financing system, medical care providers receive reimbursement according to the cost of services they provide. An alternative method of organizing health care is through health maintenance organizations (HMOs), where medical care providers receive reimbursement according to the number of patients they handle, and it is up to the providers to allocate resources between patients who receive more or fewer health care services. Adverse selection arises in insurance markets when insurance buyers know more about the risks they face than does the insurance company. As a result, the insurance company runs the risk that low-risk parties will avoid its insurance because it is too costly for them, while high-risk parties will embrace it because it looks like a good deal to them.
p220.zh: 在服务收费保健筹资制度中,医疗服务提供者根据其提供的服务费用获得补偿。组织保健的另一种方法是通过保健维持组织,根据所处理的病人人数向保健提供者报销费用,由保健提供者在接受或多或少保健服务的病人之间分配资源。 在保险市场上出现不利选择,因为保险购买者比保险公司更了解他们面临的风险。 因此,保险公司冒着风险,低风险方会因为费用太高而回避其保险,而高风险方则会接受,因为这对他们来说似乎是一笔不错的交易.

p222.original: Why is it difficult to measure health outcomes?
p222.zh: 为什么很难衡量健康结果?

p223.original: It is almost impossible to distinguish whether a health outcome such as life expectancy was the result of personal preferences that might affect health and longevity, such as diet, exercise, certain risky behavior, and consumption of certain items like tobacco, or the result of expenditures on health care (for example, annual check-ups).
p223.zh: 几乎无法区分健康结果,如预期寿命是个人偏好的结果,这些偏好可能影响健康和长寿,如饮食、锻炼、某些危险行为和消费某些物品,如烟草,还是保健支出的结果(如年度体检)。

p226.original: In an insurance system, would you expect each person to receive in benefits pretty much what they pay in premiums or is it just that the average benefits paid will equal the average premiums paid?
p226.zh: 在一个保险制度中,你是否期望每个人几乎都能得到他们支付的保险费中的福利金,或者仅仅是支付的平均福利金将等于支付的平均保险费?

p227.original: What is an actuarially fair insurance policy?
p227.zh: 精算上公平的保险单是什么?

p228.original: What is the problem of moral hazard?

p229.original: How can moral hazard lead to more costly insurance premiums than one was expected?
p229.zh: 道德风险如何导致比预期的保险费更昂贵?

p230.zh: 界定可扣减额、共同支付额和共同保险额。

p231.original: How can deductibles, copayments, and coinsurance reduce moral hazard?
p231.zh: 可扣税、共同支付和共同保险如何减少道德风险?

p232.original: What is the key difference between a fee-for-service healthcare system and a system based on health maintenance organizations?
p232.zh: 收费服务保健制度与以保健组织为基础的制度之间有什么关键区别?

p233.original: How might adverse selection make it difficult for an insurance market to operate?
p233.zh: 不利的选择如何使保险市场难以运作?

p234.original: What are some of the metrics economists use to measure health outcomes?
p234.zh: 经济学家用来衡量健康结果的一些衡量标准是什么?

p236.original: How do you think the problem of moral hazard might have affected the safety of sports such as football and boxing when safety regulations started requiring that players wear more padding?
p236.zh: 在安全规定开始要求球员佩戴更多贴纸时,你认为道德危害问题会如何影响足球和拳击等运动的安全?

p237.original: To what sorts of customers would an insurance company offer a policy with a high copay? What about a high premium with a lower copay?
p237.zh: 保险公司会给哪类客户提供高价的保单?高价和低价的公费怎么样?

p239.original: Imagine that you can divide 50-year-old men into two groups: those who have a family history of cancer and those who do not. For the purposes of this example, say that 20% of a group of 1,000 men have a family history of cancer, and these men have one chance in 50 of dying in the next year, while the other 80% of men have one chance in 200 of dying in the next year. The insurance company is selling a policy that will pay $100,000 to the estate of anyone who dies in the next year.
p239.zh: 想象一下,你可以把50岁的男性分为两类:有癌症家族史的男性和没有癌症的男性. 为了这个例子,说在1000名男子中,20%有癌症家族史,这些男子在下一年有50次死亡的机会,而另外80%的男子在下一年有200次死亡的机会。保险公司正在出售一项保险单,将支付10万美元给明年死亡的任何人的遗产.

p240.original: If the insurance company were selling life insurance separately to each group, what would be the actuarially fair premium for each group?
p240.zh: 如果保险公司将人寿保险单独出售给每个集团,那么每个集团的精算公平保费是多少?

p241.original: If an insurance company were offering life insurance to the entire group, but could not find out about family cancer histories, what would be the actuarially fair premium for the group as a whole?
p241.zh: 如果一家保险公司向整个团体提供人寿保险,但无法发现家庭癌症史,那么整个团体的精算公平保费会是多少?

p242.original: What will happen to the insurance company if it tries to charge the actuarially fair premium to the group as a whole rather than to each group separately?
p242.zh: 如果保险公司试图向整个集团而不是向每个集团分别收取精算公平的保险费,则会怎么样?
